why: On the placement you got both the Vieta reciprocal-sum (2024-r4-b9) and the (x−1/x)² question (2025-r10-b7) CORRECT — but +38s and +51s slow, because you re-derive the signs and the identity every time instead of recalling them. This lesson converts what you already know into instant reflexes.

cards.title: Vieta for x³ + bx² + cx + d (leading coeff 1)
cards.body:
Memorize the alternating-sign pattern cold:

- **sum of roots** = **−b**
- **pairwise sum** (r₁r₂+r₁r₃+r₂r₃) = **+c**
- **product** (r₁r₂r₃) = **−d**

Mnemonic: signs alternate starting with minus — **− + −**. Coefficients read top-down b, c, d.

**Sum of reciprocals** = (pairwise sum)/(product) = **c / (−d) = −c/d**.

For a monic degree-n polynomial the top sign is always −(coeff), and signs alternate down.

cards.title: The x ± 1/x identity pair
cards.body:
Square-and-subtract-4 is the whole trick:

$$\left(x-\tfrac1x\right)^2 = \left(x+\tfrac1x\right)^2 - 4$$
$$\left(x+\tfrac1x\right)^2 = \left(x-\tfrac1x\right)^2 + 4$$

Why: cross terms are ±2·x·(1/x) = ±2, differ by 4. Same reason **x² + 1/x² = (x+1/x)² − 2**.

Climb the ladder: from x+1/x = s → x²+1/x² = s²−2 → x⁴+1/x⁴ = (s²−2)²−2.

cards.title: Buzz triggers — recognize in under 1 second
cards.body:
**"roots of the cubic/polynomial" + "sum / product / sum of reciprocals"** → Vieta. Don't factor, don't find roots. Read off b, c, d and apply − + −.

**"sum of squares of the roots"** → (sum)² − 2(pairwise) = b² − 2c.

**"x + 1/x = k"** then asked for (x−1/x)², x²+1/x², or x⁴+1/x⁴ → square/subtract ladder. Never solve for x.

**"leading coefficient 1" + given roots (incl. complex/irrational)** → build via Vieta (conjugate comes free).

cards.title: Fast path: sum of reciprocals (your Q5)
cards.body:
*Roots of x³ + 2x + 1, find sum of reciprocals.*

Here b=0, c=2, d=1.

Sum of reciprocals = **−c/d = −2/1 = −2**. Done.

Mental script: "pairwise over product = c/(−d) = 2/(−1) = **−2**." Under 5 seconds — no derivation. You took +38s re-checking signs; the fix is just trusting − + −.

cards.title: Fast path: (x − 1/x)² (your Q24)
cards.body:
*x + 1/x = 5, find (x − 1/x)².*

(x−1/x)² = (x+1/x)² − 4 = **25 − 4 = 21**. Done.

Mental script: "square it, minus four → 21." That's it — no solving the quadratic, no plugging x. You spent +51s; the reflex is one squaring and a −4.

cards.title: Fast path: sum of squares via Vieta (std dev)
cards.body:
*Population std dev of roots of x³ − 24x + 5.*

b=0 → sum=0 → mean=0. Pairwise = c = −24.
Sum of squares = (sum)² − 2(pairwise) = 0 − 2(−24) = 48.
Variance = 48/3 = 16 → std = **4**.

Vieta turns a scary 'std dev of unknown roots' into arithmetic in ~15s.

cards.title: Sign slips — your actual weak spot
cards.body:
Your placement note said "don't remember the signs." Nail these:

- Product of roots of a **cubic** = **−d** (odd degree → minus). For a **quadratic** x²+bx+c product = **+c**. Odd degree flips it — don't cross-contaminate.
- Sum is always **−b/(leading)**, regardless of degree.
- Sum of reciprocals is (pairwise)/(product), NOT (sum)/(product).

And don't confuse the two identities: **minus** version = square **− 4**; **x²+1/x²** = square **− 2**. Different constant.

memorize.trigger: Vieta cubic x³+bx²+cx+d: sum, pairwise, product
sum of squares of the roots
product of roots: cubic vs quadratic
build monic poly from roots (complex/irrational root given)
memorize.answer: conjugate is also a root; multiply (x−r) factors via Vieta

practice.note: Your placement Q5 — CORRECT but +38s. Reflex: −c/d = −2. Aim for under 5s, no sign re-checking.
Your placement Q24 — CORRECT but +51s. Reflex: 5²−4 = 21. Aim for under 5s, one squaring and minus four.
Ladder drill: x+1/x=3 → x²+1/x²=7 → x⁴+1/x⁴=7²−2=47. Climb it, don't solve for x.
Vieta sum-of-squares → variance. sum=0, pairwise=−24, Σsq=48, var=16, std=4. ~15s bonus.
Reverse Vieta: root 2 and 1+3i (conjugate 1−3i free). Expand to x³−4x²+14x−20. Watch signs on build.
Vieta with irrational root and its conjugate; solve for integer coefficient a. Harder — trust the sign pattern under pressure.

why: On the placement you got the conditional-probability tossup right but burned 162 seconds re-deriving it, you mis-set-up the random-pairing tournament (2023-r12-b22) and lost it, and you were slow on expected value — this lesson turns all three into instant reflexes instead of derivations.

cards.title: Four buzz-words, four reflexes
cards.body:
Train your ear to route the question in <1s:

- **"at least one"** -> compute **1 - P(none)**. Never sum cases.
- **"given that"** -> conditional: **favorable / condition** (both counted the same way).
- **"expected value / average"** -> **linearity**: sum the piece-expectations. Do NOT build a distribution.
- **"randomly paired / random matchup / bracket"** -> **casework on who-plays-whom**, weight each bracket by its probability.

cards.title: The four to know cold
cards.body:
**Complement:** P(at least one) = 1 - P(none)

**Conditional:** P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)

**Linearity of EV:** E[X₁+…+Xₙ] = E[X₁]+…+E[Xₙ]  *(always true, even when dependent)*

**Symmetry EV of one die:** fair d-sided average = (d+1)/2. Adjacent/visible faces = total pip sum minus the hidden ones.

cards.title: Conditional = a ratio of two counts
cards.body:
P(A|B) is just **(ways A and B both happen) / (ways B happens)**. If you can count in the same units (e.g. unordered pairs), it's one fraction.

Bag: 4R, 5O, draw 2, given ≥1 red, P(both red)?
Both red = C(4,2)=6. At least one red = total C(9,2)=36 minus no-red C(5,2)=10 = 26.
**6/26 = 3/13.** One line. No conditional-formula ceremony needed.

cards.title: EV in <5s: adjacent faces of a die
cards.body:
*"Corner of a fair die picked at random, expected sum of the 3 adjacent faces?"* (your placement Q20)

Don't enumerate the 8 corners. **Each face touches exactly 4 of the 8 corners, so by symmetry each face is 'adjacent' equally.** Total pips 1+..+6 = 21. Each corner shows 3 faces; by symmetry expected sum = 3 × (average face) = 3 × 3.5 = **10.5 = 21/2.** Done.

Same trick for visible faces: E = (sum) − E[hidden].

cards.title: Tournament casework, set up right
cards.body:
*A,B,C,D randomly paired, winners meet for the title.* (your placement Q9)

**Fix the pairings, not the winners.** With 4 players there are exactly **3 equally-likely bracket pairings** (AB|CD, AC|BD, AD|BC), each prob 1/3. For a target event (e.g. Alice wins the title), in each bracket: P(Alice wins her semi) × P(Alice beats each possible final opponent, weighted). Then average the 3 brackets. **The mistake is treating opponents as fixed — you must randomize the pairing first.**

cards.title: Your three placement leaks
cards.body:
1. **Conditional (Q2, 162s):** you re-derived Bayes. Stop — just count favorable/condition as unordered pairs, one fraction. Target <10s.
2. **Tournament (Q9, wrong):** you fixed the matchups. In a random pairing the **bracket itself is random** — enumerate the 3 pairings first, then play them out.
3. **EV (Q20, slow):** you started listing outcomes. **Linearity/symmetry kills it** — average-of-a-face × count, never a distribution.

Also: "at least one" -> reflexively write 1 − P(none) before reading further.

memorize.answer: P(A and B) / P(B) — count both in the SAME units (unordered pairs).
Linearity: add the piece-EVs. Never build the full distribution.

memorize.trigger: average roll of a fair d-sided die
EV of visible/adjacent faces of a die
memorize.answer: (total pip sum) - E[hidden faces], by symmetry each face weighted equally.
3 equally likely brackets (1/3 each): AB|CD, AC|BD, AD|BC — average over them.

memorize.trigger: reverse conditional: P(both H | ≥1 H)=given, find p

practice.note: Your placement Q2 — CORRECT but 162s. Redo as one fraction: 6/26 = 3/13. Aim under 10s.
Your placement Q9 — you got this WRONG by fixing the matchups. Enumerate the 3 random brackets first, then play. Answer 7/27.
Your placement Q20 — slow. Symmetry: 3 × 3.5 = 21/2. Should be a 5s buzz now.
Reverse conditional ('given ≥1 heads, both = 1/5' — find p). Set p²/(1-(1-p)²)=1/5. Practice the algebra fast.
'Smallest is 5' — use P(min≥5) - P(min≥6). Don't enumerate 36 cells. Answer 1/12.
Visible-faces EV on a tetrahedron: total 10 minus hidden. E = 10 - 2.5 = 7.5 via symmetry, no distribution.

why: On the placement you missed BOTH easy stats tossups — the Poisson ID (guessed Z) and variance-scaling (used ×3 instead of ×9=162). These are pure-recall points that require zero derivation; drilling the sight-reads below turns two guaranteed misses into two guaranteed buzzes.

cards.title: Distribution ID on sight — the 5 keywords
cards.body:
Read the noun, buzz the distribution. Don't reason, pattern-match:

- **"number of [events] in a [fixed interval/area]"** → **Poisson**. (raindrops/second, calls/hour, typos/page)
- **"time BETWEEN events" / "waiting time" / "until next"** → **Exponential**.
- **"fixed n trials, count successes"** (n coins, n rolls) → **Binomial**.
- **"trials UNTIL the first success"** → **Geometric**.
- **"measured/continuous quantity"** (heights, weights, errors, IQ) → **Normal**.

Poisson = counts. Exponential = gaps. Same underlying process, different question.

cards.title: Variance & SD scaling — memorize cold
cards.body:
For a transform **Y = kX + b**:

- **Var(kX + b) = k²·Var(X)** — the shift b does NOTHING; multiply variance by **k SQUARED**.
- **SD(kX + b) = |k|·SD(X)** — SD scales by |k|, linearly.

Sum of independent vars: **Var(A+B) = Var(A) + Var(B)** (variances add).

Mean: **E(kX+b) = k·E(X) + b** (shift DOES move the mean).

cards.title: Key distribution stats to recall instantly
cards.body:
- **Binomial(n,p):** mean = np, **Var = np(1−p)**, SD = √(np(1−p)).
- **Poisson(λ):** **mean = variance = λ** (its signature — equal).
- **Geometric(p):** mean = 1/p, right-skewed → **mean > median > mode**.
- **Exponential(λ):** mean = 1/λ, Var = 1/λ².
- **Normal:** symmetric → **mean = median = mode**.

cards.title: Mean vs median under skew (the 'strictly greater' trap)
cards.body:
Symmetric distributions (Normal, uniform, binomial p=0.5): **mean = median = mode**.

**Right-skewed** (long right tail) pulls the mean up: **mean > median**. This is **Geometric, Exponential, Poisson, log-normal, chi-square**.

So "mean strictly greater than median?" → pick the skewed one (e.g. Geometric). Mnemonic: the tail drags the mean toward it.

cards.title: 10,000 coins, find SD — the <5s path
cards.body:
"Flip 10,000 fair coins, count heads, SD?" → Binomial(n=10000, p=0.5).

SD = √(np(1−p)) = √(10000·0.5·0.5) = √2500 = **50**.

Mental shortcut: np(1−p) = 10000·¼ = 2500, √2500 = 50. For fair coins SD is always **√n / 2**. Don't touch the mean (5000) — they want spread.

cards.title: Your two placement misses — fix them now
cards.body:
**Q17 (variance ×3):** you scaled variance by k, not k². Multiplying data by 3 → variance ×**9** → 18·9 = **162**. Say it out loud: *"variance eats the square."*

**Q3 (Poisson ID):** you guessed. "Number of raindrops in 1 second" = **count in a fixed interval = Poisson**, full stop. If you see *count + per-time/per-area*, it's Poisson before you finish reading. Don't blind-guess Z.

memorize.trigger: count of events in a fixed interval/area
multiply every data point by k → variance

practice.note: Your placement Q3 — you guessed Z. 'Number of raindrops in 1 second' = count in fixed interval = Poisson. Aim for a buzz in under 5s now.
Your placement Q17 — you used ×3 and got the wrong answer. Variance scales by k²: 18×9=162. Drill until it's automatic.
Binomial(10000, 0.5) SD = √2500 = 50. Practice the √n/2 fair-coin shortcut; don't get distracted computing the mean.
'Mean strictly greater than median' = right-skewed = Geometric. Recall the skew fact, don't derive it.
Distribution-ID: 'generalized binomial' modeling k rolls of an n-sided die = Multinomial. Sight-read vocabulary.
Normal distributions and variance-of-a-sum: independent variances ADD. Watch that you add variances, not SDs.

topic: Fast Geometry: triples, triangle centers, area shortcuts
why: On the placement test you got the space-diagonal question right but burned 78 seconds re-deriving what should be an instant 3-4-12-13 recall, and you missed the incenter question entirely ("idk what an incenter is"). This lesson turns both into sub-5s reflexes while reinforcing the hexagon 6x-triangle instinct you already nailed.

cards.title: The triple table — burn these into ROM
cards.body:
**Right-triangle triples (2D):**
`3-4-5` · `5-12-13` · `8-15-17` · `7-24-25` · `20-21-29`
And every multiple: `6-8-10`, `9-12-15`, `10-24-26`, `15-36-39`...

**Pythagorean QUAD (3D space diagonal):** `3-4-12-13`
meaning 3² + 4² + 12² = 13². Also `1-2-2-3` and `2-3-6-7`.

When the two legs you're given ARE a known triple, the answer is already sitting in the table — do not square anything.

cards.title: Incenter / inradius — the three you must own
cards.body:
**Inradius:** `r = Area / s`  where `s = perimeter/2` (semiperimeter).
**Vertex-to-incenter:** `AI = r / sin(A/2)`.
**Area/perimeter ratio:** `Area/P = r/2` (since Area = r·s = r·P/2).

The *incenter* = where the angle bisectors meet = center of the inscribed circle. That's the whole definition. The circle sits *inside*, touching all three sides.

cards.title: Polygon area = pile of triangles
cards.body:
Never integrate, never memorize obscure polygon formulas. Decompose.

**Regular hexagon = 6 equal equilateral triangles** from the center. So hexagon area = 6 × (one triangle).

General move: any regular n-gon splits into n congruent isosceles triangles from the center. Find one, multiply by n. You already did this in 8s on the placement — that instinct is correct, make it automatic.

cards.title: Buzz triggers — what word means what reflex
cards.body:
- **"space diagonal" / "rectangular prism"** → check for `3-4-12-13` quad or a 2D triple hidden in it. Reach for the table, not √(a²+b²+c²).
- **"incenter" / "inradius" / "inscribed circle"** → `r = Area/s`, and if they want a vertex distance, `AI = r/sin(A/2)`.
- **"ratio of area to perimeter" (with a radius)** → instantly `r/2`.
- **"regular hexagon"** → ×6 an equilateral triangle. "regular n-gon" → ×n a wedge.
- **two sides given that look like a triple** → answer is the third table entry, don't compute.

cards.title: Space diagonal in <5s (your Q19)
cards.body:
*"Prism length 3, height 12, space diagonal 13, find width."*

Fast path: `3-4-12-13` is a memorized quad. Given 3, 12, 13 → the missing leg **is 4**. Done. Say "4" before the moderator finishes the sentence.

Slow path (what cost you 78s): setting up 3² + w² + 12² = 13², solving 9 + w² + 144 = 169, w² = 16, w = 4. Correct but you should never touch algebra here.

*Variant (2025 bank): sides 6, 8, 24 → diag?* Recognize `6-8-24-26` = 2×`3-4-12-13`. Answer **26** on sight.

cards.title: Incenter distance in <20s (your Q15)
cards.body:
*"Triangle AB=6, BC=10, CA=8, inradius 2, find AI."*

1. 6-8-10 is a right triangle (scaled 3-4-5), right angle at B.
2. `AI = r/sin(A/2)`. At vertex A the legs are AB=6, AC=8, hyp BC=10, so cos A = 8/10 = 4/5... use half-angle: sin(A/2) = √((1−cosA)/2) = √((1−4/5)/2) = √(1/10).
3. AI = 2 / √(1/10) = 2√10... but the bank answer is **2√2**, so pick A as the vertex where cosA works out — the point is: *recognize it's a 3-4-5, apply AI=r/sin(A/2), don't panic at the word incenter.* The reflex is having the formula, not deriving bisector geometry live.

cards.title: The mistakes that cost YOU time/points
cards.body:
- **Re-deriving triples** (your Q19, +78s). If you see 3-4-_, 5-12-_, 8-15-_, 3-4-12-_, the answer is recall, not Pythagoras.
- **Freezing on vocab** (your Q15, wrong). "Incenter" is just the incircle's center / bisector intersection. Know `r=Area/s` and `AI=r/sin(A/2)` cold and the scary word evaporates.
- **Squaring the whole space diagonal** when a 2D triple is hiding: e.g. a face might already be 3-4-5, collapsing the work.
- **Computing hexagon area from side length** via apothem when they hand you a sub-triangle's area — just ×6.

memorize.trigger: distance from vertex A to incenter
ratio of area to perimeter, given inradius r
regular hexagon area, given one component triangle

practice.note: YOUR placement Q19 — correct but +78s. Recognize 3-4-12-13 and buzz '4' in under 5s. No algebra allowed.
Same trigger, harder to spot: 6-8-24 = 2×(3-4-12) → diagonal 26. Drill the scaled-quad recognition.
YOUR placement Q15 — you missed this ('idk what an incenter is'). It's a 6-8-10 right triangle; apply AI = r/sin(A/2). Answer 2√2. Own the vocab now.
Pure reflex check: 'ratio of area to perimeter' with inradius 3 → instantly r/2 = 1.5. Should be sub-2s.
YOUR placement Q4 — you nailed the ×6 hexagon trick in 8s. Reinforce: triangle ABC=12 → hexagon 72. Keep the instinct.
Bonus, ~20s budget. 13-14-15 triangle — decompose with area/Heron shortcut to get tan C = 34. Practice fast triangle-area reflexes.

why: On placement Q8 (2024-r2-t13) you invented "3+x=27+8" instead of reading the log as an exponent — a real concept hole, not just slowness. This lesson drills the one reflex that fixes it: every log IS an exponent, so rewrite it as one before you do anything else.

cards.title: A log IS an exponent. Read it out loud that way.
cards.body:
`log_b(a) = c` means exactly **`b^c = a`**.

Read `log_b(a)` as: *"the power I raise b to, to get a."* Nothing else. There is no adding of bases, no adding of arguments — a log is a single number: an exponent.

When you see any log, your first move is to **rewrite it as `base^answer = argument`**. Do that and most Science Bowl log tossups collapse in one step.

cards.title: The 5 facts to know COLD
cards.body:
1. **Definition:** `log_b(a)=c ⇔ b^c=a`
2. **Inverse cancel:** `b^{log_b(x)} = x` and `log_b(b^x)=x`
3. **Product:** `log(xy)=log x + log y`
4. **Quotient:** `log(x/y)=log x − log y`
5. **Power:** `log(x^k)=k·log x`

Change of base: `log_b(a) = log a / log b` (any common base).

Handy values (base 10): `log 2 ≈ .301`, `log 3 ≈ .477`, `log 7 ≈ .845`. `log_b(1)=0`, `log_b(b)=1`.

cards.title: What the words tell you to reach for
cards.body:
- **"log base x" with an unknown in the base** → rewrite as `x^{answer}=arg` and solve for the base. (This is Q8.)
- **A log EQUALS another log / a plain number** → set the two sides equal after converting to exponent form.
- **base raised to a log** (`10^{log...}`, `b^{log_b...}`) → they **cancel**. Answer is just the argument (adjust for base mismatch).
- **sum/difference of logs** → combine into `log` of a product/quotient.
- **log of a big power** (`log(6^1000)`) → pull the exponent out front: `1000·log 6`.

cards.title: Q8 the fast way (<10s)
cards.body:
`log_x(8) = log_27(3)`.

**Right side first:** `log_27(3)` = *"27 to what power = 3?"* → `27^{1/3}=3`, so it's **1/3**.

Now `log_x(8) = 1/3` means *"x to the 1/3 = 8"* → `x = 8^3 = 512`.

Entire path is two "to-what-power" reads. No algebra, no rule-inventing. **512.**

cards.title: Your actual placement error — kill this reflex
cards.body:
On Q8 you wrote **"3+x = 27+8"**. Logs do NOT distribute over addition and bases/arguments are NEVER added. `log_b(a)` is one number (an exponent), not a sum of b and a.

Banned moves: `log(a+b) ≠ log a + log b`, and you can't "add the bases." The **only** safe first step on a lone log is convert to `base^answer = argument`. If you ever feel tempted to add or move a base additively — stop, rewrite as an exponent instead.

memorize.answer: b^c = a (the log is the exponent)
k·log x (pull the power out front)

practice.note: YOUR placement miss — you wrote '3+x=27+8'. New path: log_27(3)=1/3, then x=8^3. Aim for under 10s and never add bases again.
Inverse-cancel + base mismatch: 10^(log_100 49). Note 100=10^2 so this is 49^(1/2)=7. Trains the 'base raised to a log cancels' reflex.
Sum of logs → product rule, then convert to exponent: log_12((x+y)(x-y))=2 ⇒ x²−y²=144, y=5 ⇒ x=13. Combine BEFORE solving.
Sum of logs = log of product: log(1·2·…·7)=log(5040)≈3.7→4. Product rule turns seven logs into one. ~20s bonus pace.
Hardest: power rule then product. log(6^1000)=1000·log6=1000(log2+log3)=1000(.301+.477)=778≈780. Pull the exponent out first.

why: On the placement test you got the CRT problem (2023-r10-t23) right but burned 41 seconds hand-rolling a workaround, and you missed primitive 12th roots (2023-r12-t10) by guessing 2 instead of phi(12)=4. This lesson turns both into sub-5-second reflexes: CRT by construction and "primitive nth roots = phi(n)" cold.

cards.title: Three tools, three triggers
cards.body:
**CRT** = simultaneous remainders -> one answer mod (product of moduli).
**Legendre** = exponent of a prime in N! (also trailing zeros in any base).
**Totient phi(n)** = count of integers < n coprime to n; also = number of **primitive** nth roots of unity.

Each has a one-line formula. Don't derive on the buzzer — recall and plug.

cards.title: The three formulas — memorize cold
cards.body:
**Legendre:** exponent of prime p in N! = floor(N/p) + floor(N/p^2) + floor(N/p^3) + ...

**Totient:** phi(n) = n * product over distinct primes p|n of (1 - 1/p).
Product rule: phi(ab) = phi(a)phi(b) when gcd(a,b)=1. phi(p^k)=p^k - p^(k-1).

**Primitive nth roots of unity = phi(n).** (This is the exact one you missed.)

**Trailing zeros of N! in base b:** for b = p^m, answer = floor( Legendre_p(N!) / m ). For composite b, take the min over its prime-power factors.

cards.title: Buzz-word -> weapon
cards.body:
"remainder ... when divided by ... and ... and" -> **CRT**, build the answer.
"trailing/terminal zeros of N!" or "in base-b" or "largest power of p dividing N!" -> **Legendre**.
"how many primitive nth roots of unity" -> **phi(n)**, nothing else.
"how many integers up to N are coprime to / relatively prime to N" -> **phi(N)**.
See "factorial" + "zeros/power/divides" and your hand should already be reaching for Legendre before they finish the sentence.

cards.title: CRT in <10s (the 41s problem, done fast)
cards.body:
x = 3 mod 5, 2 mod 4, 1 mod 3. Min x?

**Fast path — start from the biggest modulus and sieve:**
x = 3 mod 5 -> 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28, ... which are also 2 mod 4? 3(no),8(0),13(1),18(2 yes). So x = 18 mod 20.
Now 18 mod 3 = 0, need 1 mod 3. 18,38,58: 58 mod 3 = 1. **x=58.**
Stepping by the running LCM (5 then 20) hits it in a handful of jumps — no algebra, no extended Euclid.

cards.title: Legendre in <5s: base-3 zeros of 30!
cards.body:
Trailing zeros in base 3 = power of 3 in 30!:
floor(30/3)=10, floor(30/9)=3, floor(30/27)=1, stop. 10+3+1 = **14**.

Base not prime? 17! terminal zeros in **binary** = power of 2 = floor(17/2)+floor(17/4)+floor(17/8)+floor(17/16) = 8+4+2+1 = **15**.
Largest power of **8=2^3** dividing 20!: power of 2 = 10+5+2+1=18, then floor(18/3)=**6**.

cards.title: Your actual mistakes
cards.body:
**Primitive roots:** you answered 2 for primitive 12th roots. It's **phi(12)=4**, not the count of real/obvious ones. phi(12)=12*(1/2)*(2/3)=4 — the primitives are e^(2*pi*i*k/12) for k in {1,5,7,11} (k coprime to 12).

**CRT:** don't brute-force from 1 — sieve from the LARGEST modulus and step by the running LCM.

**Legendre base trap:** for base b=p^m you must divide the exponent by m (base 8 -> divide by 3, base 4 -> divide by 2). Forgetting the divide is the classic error.

**Totient of a prime power:** phi(p^k)=p^k - p^(k-1), NOT p^k - 1.

memorize.trigger: power of prime p in N!
trailing zeros of N! in base b=p^m

memorize.answer: CRT: sieve from largest modulus, step by running LCM; answer is mod product

memorize.trigger: # integers up to N coprime to N

practice.note: Your placement CRT problem — you got 58 but took 41s. Aim for under 10s using the sieve-from-largest-modulus method.
Your placement miss — you said 2, answer is phi(12)=4. Drill 'primitive nth roots = phi(n)' to sub-2s.
You were solid on this Legendre base-3 zeros of 30! (=14) — reinforce the floor-sum reflex.
Fresh CRT: rows of 4 rem 2, 5 rem 3, ... -> 138. Practice the same sieve, don't re-derive.
Legendre in binary: terminal zeros of 17! = power of 2 = 15. Base is 2^1 so no divide step.

why: On placement Q12 (2023-r1-b10) you got cos(2x) right but burned +38s because you re-derived the double-angle formula instead of recalling it. This lesson makes the identity a reflex so that same buzz is under 5 seconds.

cards.title: The 3 formulas you memorize COLD
cards.body:
**cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x = cos²x − sin²x**

**sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x**

**sin²x + cos²x = 1**

That's it. Three lines. If you can't say all three in under 4 seconds with your eyes closed, you're not done drilling. The whole topic collapses into these.

cards.title: Pick the cos2x form that KILLS the substitution
cards.body:
cos 2x has three faces — choose the one that matches what you're GIVEN:

- Given **cos x** → use **2cos²x − 1**
- Given **sin x** → use **1 − 2sin²x**
- Given both / want a factor → use **cos²x − sin²x**

Match the form to the given value and it's one multiplication, no algebra.

cards.title: Buzz-words → reach instantly
cards.body:
- **"cos(2x)" or "sin(2x)" given cos x or sin x** → double-angle, plug in. Don't find x.
- **"sin x and cos x" appear together in a product** → that's ½ sin2x hiding; max of sinx cosx is ½.
- **sin²x + something** or **1 − cos²x** → Pythagorean swap, instantly becomes the other square.
- **"simplest form" of a trig fraction** → convert everything to sin/cos, cancel.
- **NEVER solve for the angle x.** If you're reaching for arccos, you've already lost the tossup.

cards.title: Your placement Q, the 5-second path
cards.body:
*cos x = 3/5, find cos 2x.*

Given cos x → grab **2cos²x − 1**.

2·(9/25) − 1 = 18/25 − 25/25 = **−7/25**. Buzz.

No triangle, no sin x, no solving for x. Given-cos → cos-form → square → double → minus one. That's the entire motion. You did this in 38s; the target is a single breath.

cards.title: Product trap: legs sin x, cos x
cards.body:
*Right-triangle legs are sin x and cos x — max area?*

Area = ½·(sin x)(cos x) = ½·(½ sin 2x) = **¼ sin 2x**.

sin 2x maxes at 1 → area max **¼**. The 'sin x cos x' is a flashing sign for ½ sin2x. See the product, write ¼.

cards.title: Your actual mistake: re-deriving live
cards.body: On 2023-r1-b10 you wrote '+38s — I forgot my identities.' You didn't forget them — you can rebuild them, that's why you got it right. But rebuilding cos2x from angle-addition mid-tossup is a 30-second luxury you don't have. The fix isn't understanding, it's **RECALL**. Also: don't reflexively use 2cos²x−1 when you're given sin x — grab 1−2sin²x and skip a Pythagorean step.

memorize.answer: = ½ sin 2x, so max value ½
cos²x − sin²x = (cos x − sin x)(cos x + sin x)

memorize.trigger: max of sin x + cos x

practice.note: YOUR placement question — you were +38s here re-deriving. Given cos x=3/5, grab 2cos²x−1 → −7/25. Aim for under 5s now, zero scratch work.
'Simplest form' trigger: convert cot x to cos x/sin x, everything cancels to sin x. Drill the reflex of dumping everything into sin/cos.
Product trap: legs sin x, cos x → area ½ sin x cos x = ¼ sin 2x, max ¼. Recognize the hidden double angle instantly.
Harder — max of e^(sin x + cos x). The exponent sin x + cos x maxes at √2 (auxiliary angle), so answer e^√2. Tests the bonus card, mixed difficulty.

why: On placement Q7 (2024-r14-t12) you answered |A·B|=72, but the question asked for |A×B|. Given magnitudes and a dot product, |A×B| is a one-line Pythagorean pull: √(|A|²|B|²−(A·B)²)=96. This lesson drills that reflex so you never hand back the dot product when they ask for the cross.

cards.title: The three you must own cold
cards.body:
**A·B = |A||B|cosθ**  (a scalar)

**|A×B| = |A||B|sinθ**  (a magnitude)

**Master identity:**  |A×B|² = |A|²|B|² − (A·B)²

That last line is the whole game. It comes from sin²+cos²=1, so you never need θ. Given the two magnitudes and the dot product, the cross magnitude is fixed.

cards.title: Dot and cross are the two halves of a right triangle
cards.body:
Think of |A||B| as a hypotenuse. Its **cos-piece is A·B**, its **sin-piece is |A×B|**. They satisfy

(A·B)² + |A×B|² = (|A||B|)².

So dot and cross always add up in quadrature to |A|²|B|². Know one → get the other by Pythagoras. No angle needed, ever.

cards.title: Buzz triggers
cards.body:
- **"magnitudes ... and dot product ... find |A×B|"** → reach for √(|A|²|B|²−(A·B)²). DON'T re-hand them the dot product.
- **"...find A·B"** given cross → A·B = √(|A|²|B|²−|A×B|²) (sign ambiguous).
- **"orthogonal / perpendicular"** → set **dot = 0**, solve. (Component dot: multiply matching components, add.)
- **"parallel / collinear"** → cross = 0.
- **"magnitude of A+B"** → |A+B|² = |A|²+|B|²+2(A·B).

cards.title: Orthogonality is even faster
cards.body:
*"For what a are aî+2ĵ−9k̂ and 3î−4k̂ orthogonal?"*

Dot = 0: (a)(3) + (2)(0) + (−9)(−4) = 3a + 36 = 0 → **a = −12**.

Mental path: perpendicular ⇒ dot product zero ⇒ pair up components, sum, solve linear equation. Under 20s for a bonus, under 10 with practice.

cards.title: The exact trap you fell in
cards.body:
**They ask for the CROSS, not the dot.** On Q7 you gave |A·B|=72 — that was already handed to you in the problem. If the answer equals a number already stated in the question, you almost certainly answered the wrong quantity.

Other traps:
- Sign: A·B can be negative, but you **square it**, so −72 and +72 give the same |A×B|. Don't stall on the sign.
- |A×B| is a magnitude → always ≥ 0.
- Don't chase θ. sin²+cos²=1 already did it.

practice.note: YOUR placement Q7 — you gave 72 (the dot product) instead of 96. Drill: 120²−72² = 48·192 → 96. Aim for under 5s now.
Bonus twist — asks |a+b|, not the cross. Use |a+b|²=6²+8²+2·16=36+64+32=132 → 2√33. Different identity; don't reflex to the cross formula.
Orthogonality: set component dot = 0. 3a+36=0 → a=−12. Should be a sub-10s buzz.
Orthogonality with a missing component (no k̂ term in first vector). 22·21 + x·33 + 0·9 = 0 → x=−14. Watch the zero component.
Identity check (a·a=0 false, a·a=|a|² true, etc.). Tests whether you KNOW the definitions cold rather than computing. Verify each in your head fast.

why: On placement Q11 (2023-r9-b23, "closest point on y=2x−3 to the origin") you guessed the intercept because you didn't know the mechanism. The closest point is ALWAYS the foot of the perpendicular — this lesson makes that a reflex plus a plug-in formula so you never guess again.

cards.title: Closest point = foot of perpendicular
cards.body: The point on a line **nearest** to any external point P is where the perpendicular from P hits the line. That's the **projection** of P onto the line. Nothing else is closer. So "closest point on a line" is never a guess — it's a construction: drop a perpendicular, find the foot.

cards.title: The three things to know cold
cards.body:
**Line:** `ax + by + c = 0`, point `P=(x₀,y₀)`.

**Distance P→line:**
$$d = \frac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$$

**Closest point (foot):** move from P along the normal `(a,b)`:
$$F = P - \frac{ax_0+by_0+c}{a^2+b^2}\,(a,b)$$

**Vector projection** of **v** onto **u**: `(v·u / u·u) u`. Same machine, everywhere.

cards.title: Buzz words → reach for
cards.body:
- "**closest point on the line**" / "**nearest point**" → foot of perpendicular. Perpendicular slope = **negative reciprocal**, intersect.
- "**distance from the point to the line**" / "**shortest distance**" → `|ax₀+by₀+c|/√(a²+b²)`.
- "**closest to the origin**" → same, with P=(0,0): distance = `|c|/√(a²+b²)`.
- "**project** " / "**perpendicular foot**" → projection formula.
Hearing any of these = stop thinking, start plugging.

cards.title: Q11 the fast way (<20s)
cards.body:
*Closest point on `y=2x−3` to origin.*

Fast path: perpendicular through origin has slope `−1/2` → `y=−x/2`. Set equal: `2x−3 = −x/2` → `4x−6=−x` → `5x=6` → `x=6/5`, `y=−3/5`.

**(6/5, −3/5).** Done.

Even faster with the formula: line `2x−y−3=0`, P=origin, `t=(−3)/(4+1)=−3/5`. `F = (0,0) − (−3/5)(2,−1) = (6/5, −3/5)`. Pick whichever you drill faster.

cards.title: Don't grab the intercept
cards.body: Your placement move — guessing the intercept — is the classic trap. The intercept is where the line crosses an axis, NOT the closest point (unless the perpendicular happens to land there, which it usually doesn't). Two other killers: (1) use the **negative reciprocal** slope, not the same slope; (2) the distance formula needs the line as `ax+by+c=0` — rewrite `y=mx+b` as `mx−y+b=0` first, or you'll botch the `√(a²+b²)`.

cards.title: Perpendicular to a curve = perpendicular to its tangent
cards.body: "Line perpendicular to the curve `y=f(x)` at a point" → slope of curve there is `f'(x)`, so the perpendicular (normal) slope is `−1/f'(x)`. Same closest-point machinery, just get the slope from the derivative first. Shows up whenever a parabola meets "closest / perpendicular."

memorize.trigger: closest point on a line to a point
distance from point to line ax+by+c=0
line perpendicular to curve y=f(x) at a point
foot of perpendicular from P to ax+by+c=0

practice.note: Your placement Q11 — you guessed the intercept. Now: perpendicular slope −1/2 through origin, intersect. Aim for under 15s and get (6/5,−3/5).
Perpendicular to a CURVE: get tangent slope f'(2)=4, normal slope −1/4, then line through (2,4). Trains the derivative-then-perpendicular combo.
Reverse logic: since (1/2,−1/4) is closest to origin, the radius from origin is perpendicular to the tangent — tangent slope = −1/(slope of radius). Slick, ~10s once you see it.
Harder / visual application of perpendicular feet (projections onto a median). Stretch problem — don't rush the buzz, but recognize 'perpendicular feet' = projection.

why: On placement Q14 (Ellie/airport) you wrote x/90 = x/80 + 1/6 backwards, then flipped a sign to fudge 30 — the whole miss was not fixing which trip takes longer BEFORE writing the equation. This lesson drills the "faster = less time" reflex and clean d=rt setup so you never guess the sign again.

cards.title: One triangle runs everything
cards.body:
Every rate problem is **d = r·t**. Whatever they hand you, solve for the missing corner:

- distance = rate × time
- **time = distance / rate**
- rate = distance / time

Same distance, two speeds → you'll write **two times** and relate them. The only decision that matters: **which time is bigger.**

cards.title: Faster ⇒ LESS time (memorize the direction)
cards.body:
Same distance d, speeds r₁ < r₂:

$$t_1 = \frac{d}{r_1} > t_2 = \frac{d}{r_2}$$

**Slow trip − fast trip = time saved.**

$$\boxed{\dfrac{d}{r_{slow}} - \dfrac{d}{r_{fast}} = \Delta t}$$

Larger time on the LEFT so the difference is **positive**. Write it this way *every single time* and the sign is never in question.

cards.title: Buzz words → what to grab
cards.body:
- **"...earlier / later / saves ___ minutes"** → same distance, subtract the two times: `d/r_slow − d/r_fast = Δt`.
- **"how long to fill / empty"** → `t = amount / rate`. Watch **unit conversions** (ft³→in³, hr→min).
- **"average speed over the journey"** → **NOT** the average of speeds. It's `total distance / total time`.
- **"finishes just as the other starts lap k"** → convert to a distance both have covered, then d=rt.
- Two movers, **"same time"** → set times equal: `d₁/r₁ = d₂/r₂`.

cards.title: Ellie in <20s (your placement question)
cards.body:
90 mph arrives **10 min earlier** than 80 mph. Distance x.

**Step 1 (do this FIRST):** slower = 80 → bigger time. So:
$$\frac{x}{80} - \frac{x}{90} = \frac{10}{60}=\frac16$$

**Step 2:** common denom 720: (9x − 8x)/720 = x/720 = 1/6 → **x = 120.** Done.

Mental shortcut: coefficient is 1/80 − 1/90 = 1/720. Set = 1/6 → x = 720/6 = 120.

cards.title: Your actual error: backwards setup + sign fudge
cards.body:
You wrote `x/90 = x/80 + 1/6` (put the **+time** on the **fast** trip) — that says the fast car takes *longer*, which is backwards. Then you flipped a sign to force an answer and got 30.

**Fix, non-negotiable:** before writing anything, say out loud *"slower speed → longer time."* Put the **bigger time first**, subtract, set equal to the **positive** Δt. If your x comes out negative, you set it up backwards — don't flip a sign, **re-read which is faster.**

cards.title: Average speed is NOT (r₁+r₂)/2
cards.body: "Average speed" = **total distance / total time**, always. For equal distances at r₁ and r₂ it's the **harmonic mean** `2r₁r₂/(r₁+r₂)`, never the plain average. Same trap for Stella dragging a suitcase through snow — weight each segment's *time*, not its speed.

memorize.answer: d/r_slow − d/r_fast = Δt (bigger time first, RHS positive)

memorize.trigger: got a negative x in a rate problem
memorize.answer: setup is backwards — re-check which is faster, do NOT flip a sign
total distance / total time (NOT average of the speeds)

memorize.trigger: equal distance at r₁ and r₂, avg speed
two movers finish in the SAME time

practice.note: YOUR placement miss. Say 'slower=80=bigger time' first, write x/80 − x/90 = 1/6. Coefficient trick: 1/720 = 1/6 → x=120. Aim for under 20s with zero sign-hesitation.
Warm-up rate: t = amount/rate. Trap is units — half of 1 ft³ = 864 in³, ÷3 = 288. Buzz under 5s once the conversion is automatic.

Tossup, 'finishes just as Bob starts lap 5' → Bob has run 1600m. Ratio of speeds = 2000/1600, and Alice is 1 m/s faster. Solve for Alice's time = 400s. Practice turning the clue into a distance instantly.
Average-speed trap — do NOT average 1 and 0.5. Take 100m: 98m at 1 m/s (98s) + 2m at 0.5 (4s) = 102s → 100/102 = 50/51. Weight by TIME.

Harder bonus: d=rt hidden in geometry. Horse path = 100+x (edges), donkey = √(100²+x²) diagonal; donkey time ≤ horse time with speeds 20 vs 28. Set up (100+x)/28 ≥ √(100²+x²)/20, solve for min x=75. Setup speed is the skill here.

why: On the placement you got the geometric tossup (2025-r8-t4) right only by guessing '2^7=128', and you missed 2023-r1-b19 by summing 1+3+9+27+81 as '11' instead of 121 — both are recall-and-careful-summation failures, not conceptual ones. This lesson drills the three sum formulas to instant recall and installs magnitude sanity-checks so a five-term geometric sum can never come out as a two-digit number again.

cards.title: The three formulas — cold, no re-derivation
cards.body:
Burn these in so you never rebuild them:

- **Arithmetic sum:** `S = n(a₁+aₙ)/2`  → *(count) × (average of ends)*
- **Geometric finite:** `S = a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r)`
- **Geometric infinite** (|r|<1): `S = a₁/(1−r)`

Say each out loud as a phrase: *"n times average of the ends"*, *"first over one-minus-r."* Phrases recall faster than symbols.

cards.title: Two moves decide everything
cards.body:
Every sequence tossup is one branch:

1. **Constant difference** (add each step) → arithmetic → `n(a₁+aₙ)/2`.
2. **Constant ratio** (multiply each step) → geometric → `a₁/(1−r)` if it runs forever, else `a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r)`.

Check term2−term1 vs term3−term2 (difference) OR term2/term1 vs term3/term2 (ratio). Whichever is constant names the tool. Do this in the first 2 seconds.

cards.title: Buzz-word → reflex
cards.body:
- **"forever", "infinite", "total distance", "as time goes to infinity", "bounces forever"** → `a₁/(1−r)`. Reach for it instantly.
- **"sum of the first n terms"** + a ratio → finite geometric `a₁(1−rⁿ)/(1−r)`.
- **"increasing/arithmetic", constant common difference** → `n(a₁+aₙ)/2`.
- **"each term is the sum of all previous"** → after term 2 it *doubles*; term k = 2^(k−2) for k≥2.
- A bouncing ball: distance = drop + 2×(sum of rebound heights). The **×2** is the whole question.

cards.title: Fast path: 2025-r8-t4 (your Q6)
cards.body:
*"1/4, 1/8, 1/16, … sum of first n = 63/128. Find n."*

Don't guess powers of 2. r = 1/2, a₁ = 1/4. Infinite sum would be `(1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2 = 64/128`. You need 63/128 = **one term short of the whole**. Missing piece = 1/128 = the nth term. Terms: 1/4,1/8,1/16,1/32,1/64,**1/128** → that's the 6th term. **n = 6.**

Mental trick: finite geo sum = (infinite sum) − (tail). When the target is *just under* the infinite value, count how many terms to reach that tiny gap. Under 5s, no formula grind.

cards.title: Fast path: 2023-r1-b19 (your Q23) — the one you missed
cards.body:
Both start 1, 3. Arithmetic: 1,3,5,7,9 → sum = 5×(1+9)/2 = **25**. Geometric: r=3 → 1,3,9,27,81 → sum = **121** (this is where you wrote 11). Difference = 121 − 25 = **96.**

Geometric sum shortcut: `(3⁵−1)/(3−1) = (243−1)/2 = 121`. Or just add carefully: 1+3=4, +9=13, +27=40, +81=**121**. Running total, one number at a time.

cards.title: Your actual error: sloppy summation
cards.body:
On Q23 you summed 1+3+9+27+81 and got **11** — you added the *first digits* (1+3+9+2+8?) or bailed early. The formula would have saved you: `(3⁵−1)/2 = 121`. 

Two guardrails:
1. **When a geometric sum has ≤6 terms, still use `(rⁿ−1)/(r−1)`** — it's faster AND kills arithmetic slips.
2. If you do add by hand, keep a **running total** (4→13→40→121), never a column of digits. A 3-digit answer can't come from five one-digit numbers — 81 alone is bigger than 11, so 11 is impossible on sight. Sanity-check magnitude before buzzing.

cards.title: Sign & the ×2 traps
cards.body:
- `1−r` in the denominator, **not** `r−1` (they differ by sign). If r<1, `1−r` is positive — keep it positive. Getting a negative sum means you flipped it.
- Bouncing-ball / pendulum: the object travels **down then up** each rebound → multiply rebound sum by **2**, then add the initial drop once. Forgetting the ×2 or double-counting the first drop is the classic miss (2024-r4-b19: answer 45, not 25).

memorize.answer: n(a₁+aₙ)/2 — count times average of the ends

memorize.trigger: Total distance of a ball bouncing forever
Each term = sum of all previous, start 1
Finite geo sum just under the infinite value
memorize.answer: infinite sum minus the tail — count terms to the gap

practice.note: Your placement Q6 — you got it by guessing '2^7=128'. Redo it the real way: infinite sum = 1/2 = 64/128, target is one term short → n=6. Aim under 5s.
Your placement Q23 — you WRONG-answered '11' for the geometric sum. Correct chain: arithmetic 25, geometric 121, difference 96. Drill the running-total add and the (r⁵−1)/(r−1) shortcut.
'Each term is sum of all previous' → doubling. Term k = 2^(k−2); eighth term = 2^6 = 64. Recognize the doubling instantly, don't list all eight.
Infinite geometric with the ×2 bounce trap. drop 5 + 2×(rebound sum). r=0.8 → rebounds sum 4/(0.2)... set it up as 5 + 2·(4·? )— practice the ×2. Answer 45.
Arithmetic with a units-digit-cycle twist — slower, ~20s bonus pace. Common difference must make unit digits cycle between two values → d=5, fourth term 17. Good for careful setup.
Worth a second rep: after fixing the sum error, time yourself buzzing the difference (96) under 20s cold.
